id_and_class.summary: George Berkeley holds that nothing exists but minds (spirits) and the ideas they perceive: to be is to be perceived or to perceive. Sensible objects are stable, lawful collections of ideas, not mind-independent matter behind them. God, an infinite spirit, causes and sustains these ideas, which keeps the sensory world vivid, ordered, public, and in existence when no finite mind perceives it.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: To Be Is to Be Perceived or to Perceive

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Phenomenal consciousness is the immediate apprehension of ideas by active finite spirits, and it is the mode in which the sensible world itself exists, not an inner representation of something beyond it.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Bodies, including one's own, are collections of ideas in minds. There is no material substance, so the mind-body problem becomes a relation between active spirits and the passive ideas they perceive.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Not applicable (spirits and ideas are the only basic categories; there is no matter for consciousness to emerge from)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: The subject is an active spirit that perceives and wills. A spirit is never itself an idea, since ideas are passive, and it is known by a reflective ‘notion’ of its own perceiving and willing, not by sensory presentation.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Qualities such as redness, warmth, and sweetness are the very fabric of sensible things. Berkeley's likeness principle holds that an idea can resemble only another idea, so experienceless matter could never explain them.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Finite spirits; ideas (of sense, reflection, memory, and imagination); God as infinite spirit; no material substance and no abstract ideas.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Immediate perception gives ideas directly; reflection gives a notion of one's own mind; the existence of God is inferred from the involuntary, ordered character of sensory ideas.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Two categories: active spirits and passive ideas. Ordinary objects, such as an apple, are clusters of visual, tactile, olfactory, gustatory, and affective ideas habitually conjoined and given one name.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Sensory experience; perception of space and distance; the self as active spirit; the objectivity of the external world.
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Esse est percipi aut percipere, combined with divine causation: ideas cannot cause one another and finite spirits do not will most of them, so God produces the sensory order.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: Ideas exist in minds, finite and infinite. Sensible things persist unperceived by humans because they remain in God's perception.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: Only spirits are causes. Finite spirits cause their imaginings by will, while God causes sensory ideas, which are involuntary, vivid, coherent, and shared.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: Objects are unified by the habitual conjunction of ideas across senses. Phenomenal space is an ordered field of sensory ideas calibrated across sight and touch through experience.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Berkeley rejects representationalism. In vision, visible appearances work as signs that suggest tactile experiences, a learned, language-like relation he later calls a divine visual language.
core_claims_and_evidence: An idea can resemble only another idea, so the representationalist view that ideas copy unperceived matter is unintelligible.
Primary qualities such as size, shape, and motion vary with the perceiver just as colors and tastes do, so the primary-secondary distinction collapses.
Visual distance and magnitude are learned through correlations between visual and tactile ideas, as argued in the New Theory of Vision.
The involuntary, lawful order of sensory ideas requires an infinite spirit as their cause.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Philosophical argument and phenomenological analysis of perception, with an explicitly theological aim.

empirics_and_critiques.known_empirical_interventions_or_tests: Berkeley's theory of vision, that spatial depth and magnitude are learned through cross-modal association with touch, is an empirical psychological claim about perception.
empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: Divine causation carries much of the explanatory burden. The ontology of active spirits is less accessible than the ontology of ideas, since all immediate objects of knowledge are ideas. Identifying ordinary objects with collections of ideas is hard to reconcile with contemporary scientific realism.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: How active minds are known if knowledge is of ideas, and what a ‘notion’ of spirit amounts to, remain the least developed parts of the view.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Coherent as a two-category ontology of spirits and ideas. It keeps empirical realism for ordinary life while denying metaphysical realism about matter, and avoids solipsism by grounding the public world in God.

AI_consciousness.rationale: Only spirits perceive and act, and a machine is a collection of ideas, so a machine as such could not be conscious on this view.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: A spirit is not an idea and so is not part of the body that dies, and Berkeley's system is built to support religious belief, though survival is not argued here.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: Berkeley directs his project to practice and morality, starting from the nearness and omnipresence of God, whose will orders the whole sensory world.

virtual_immortality.rationale: A digital copy would be only a further collection of ideas, never an active perceiving spirit.
